---
title: "Appendix C: Personas, capabilities and relational indicators"
---

The main text uses the capabilities approach to construct personas. This appendix supplies supporting evidence for capability choices and the technical operations that define relational indicators.

## Overview of personas

Personas represent birds, lizards, and urban trees. Table 1 provides further information about each persona. The table describes example species while demonstrating how personas cover distinct lifespans, body sizes, and forms of social life.

‘Birds’ persona includes woodland birds, including red-rumped parrot (Psephotus haematonotus) and Superb fairywren (Malurus cyaneus), represent social, intelligent canopy dwellers [^6]. Their urban colonisation demonstrates behavioural plasticity through social learning that evolves into persistent cultures [^23].

‘Lizards’ persona includes ground-dwelling lizards, such as Eastern blue-tongued lizard (Tiliqua scincoides), indicate movement patterns. Lizards require interconnected ground-level habitat mosaics. In Melbourne, roadways and buildings significantly constrain their movement [^10].

‘Trees’ persona includes large old trees, including river red gums (Eucalyptus camaldulensis) and English elms (Ulmus sp.), represent a particular life stage. Evidence increasingly shows their problem-solving strategies and social function [^14]. In urban contexts, humans aggressively prune these trees and deprive them of their tree- fungi connections [^9].

**Table 1. Persona details**

|  | **Bird** | **Lizard** | **Tree** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Representative Species** | Red-rumped parrot (*Psephotus haematonotus*; Superb fairywren (*Malurus cyaneus*) | Eastern blue-tongued lizard (*Tiliqua scincoides*); Victorian Grassland Earless Dragon (*Tympanocryptis pinguicolla*) | River red gum (*Eucalyptus camaldulensis*); English elm (*Ulmus* sp.) |
| **Body size** | 13–28 cm long;  8–77 g mass | 18–60 cm long;  0.2–0.9 kg mass | 20 m crown width;  1,000 kg mass[^1] |
| **Lifespan** | 5–23 years | 15–30 years | Woodland: 500–1,000 years[^2] (senescent features after ~180 years[^3]);  Street: 20–95 years[^4] |
| **Reproduction** | 3–7 eggs/clutch;  1–3 broods/year;  Nest in shrubs and tree hollows | 10–20 live young;  Every second year;  Nest in fallen logs | Woodlands: 300,000–400,000 seeds kg⁻¹;  Street: reliant on humans for reproduction[^4] |
| **Communication** | Songs, calls, visual displays, flock cohesion | Tongue-flicks, head-bobs, chemical marks | Volatiles, root exudates, branch drops, mycorrhizal signalling[^5] |
| **Problem-solving** | Cultural adoption, social learning[^6] | Trial-and-error learning, direct experience[^7] | Growth, mycorrhizal signalling, epigenetic shifts[^8] |
| **Socialisation** | Family groups: 3–5;  Flocks: 10–100 | Solitary except mating;  Density: 1–2 adults/ha | Woodland: mycorrhizal networks link hundreds of trees[^9]; Street: isolated[^9] |
| **Horizontal space use** | Territory: 50–200 m²[^10] | Home range: 50–130 m radius[^10] | Woodland: Roots extend 10–20 m; seeds fall < 100 m but may drift km in floods[^11]; Street: significantly less |
| **Vertical space use** | Use tree canopies 0–45m tall | Spend >75% time under crevices, rocks, and logs;  Forage in shrubs and grasses. [^10] | Roots: 0–1 m deep;  Canopy: ≤45 m tall[^1] |
| **Key barriers** | Roads >15 m;  High glass façades[^10] | Roads >5 m;  Walls, solid fences[^10] | Compacted soil, paving [^9] |
| **Dwelling requirements** | Dense mid-storey, hollows, open lawns[^10] | Connected vegetation, coarse debris, warm basking spots[^10] | Open soil to regenerate, space to grow and decay[^12] |
| **Primary threats** | Canopy loss, early hollow removal | Fragmentation, cats/dogs, roads | Removal of senescent trees, no natural recruitment, severed mycorrhizal links |


## Overview of capabilities

We next sample capabilities across birds, lizards, and trees. The tables below show capabilities for birds, lizards, and trees respectively. Capabilities marked with an asterisk (\*) indicate the subset we model using relational indicators.

We organise capability choices across two domains. The first domain covers scale: individual life, collective interaction, and multiple generations. The second domain uses Schlosberg's framework of health, autonomy, and affiliation [^13]. This framework extends the capabilities approach from individuals to communities and ecosystems.

These capabilities demonstrate how lizards, birds, and trees participate in multispecies communities, hold knowledge, innovate, and contribute to urban living. We understand these contributions as 'design', which we define as the collective creation of conditions that support life in response to novel circumstances [^14]. To illustrate this concept, we include columns showing how capabilities create services for each persona as well as for others.

**Table 2. Sample bird capabilities**

| Capability | Service to Self | Service to Others | Threats | Domain | Scale |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Forage\* | Forage on invertebrates and nectar | Support pollination[^15] and pest control | Young and non-native trees lack insect-attracting branches | Health | Individual life |
| Bathe | Bathe and drink in freshwater sources , maintain feather condition, hydration | Seed dispersal via mud on feet | Water pollution, lack of water sources | Health | Individual life |
| Move | Avoid predators, access resources | Provide seed rain that accelerates forest succession[^16] | Collisions with buildings, wind turbines | Health | Individual life |
| Explore | Establish own home range | Regulate gene flow in populations | Habitat fragmentation, barriers | Autonomy | Individual life |
| Defend | Defend territory from threats | Maintain ecosystem balance | Invasive species, human disturbance | Autonomy | Collective interaction |
| Socialise\* | Rest in communal roosting sites | Provide droppings that can enrich soil[^17], combat fragmentation at forest edges through endozoochory[^18] | Pruning for safety removes suitable roosts | Affiliation | Collective interaction |
| Learn | Develop and express local dialects | Indicate ecosystem health to humans | Noise pollution, population isolation | Affiliation | Collective interaction |
| Procreate\* | Access nesting sites for breeding | Create structures used by other species | Natural hollows take centuries to form | Affiliation | Multiple generations |

**Table 3. Sample lizard capabilities**

| Capability | Service to Self | Service to Others | Threats | Domain | Scale |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Thermoregulate | Use warm and cool spots to stabilise body | Create nutrient patches through droppings at bask sites | Lack of diverse thermal environments | Health | Individual life |
| Forage\* | Secure food in low vegetation and canopy debris | Regulate insect populations[^10] | Pesticide use, lack of prey | Health | Individual life |
| Drink | Maintain bodily functions | Contribute to small-scale water cycles | Water pollution, lack of water sources | Health | Individual life |
| Shelter\* | Use logs and fallen trees for cover and nesting | Build micro‑refugia used by others | Ground debris cleared by management regimes | Health | Multiple generations |
| Move | Access various resources | Seed dispersal, nutrient distribution | Habitat fragmentation, roads | Autonomy | Collective interaction |
| Defend | Defend territories and secure resources | Maintain population distribution | Habitat loss, invasive species | Autonomy | Collective interaction |
| Seek shelter from threats | Avoid predation, harsh conditions | Create burrows used by other species | Removal of ground cover, debris | Autonomy | Collective interaction |
| Socialise | Establish hierarchies | Indicate ecosystem health to researchers | Isolation of populations | Affiliation: | Collective interaction |
| Explore\* | Traverse routes to reach mates | Maintain gene flow | Inbreeding due to isolation | Affiliation | Collective interaction |

**Table 4. Sample Tree capabilities**

| Capability | Service to Self | Service to Others | Threats | Domain | Scale |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Perform photosynthesis | Produce energy for growth | Produce oxygen, sequester carbon | Air pollution, shading from buildings | Health | Individual life |
| Access water and nutrients | Sustain growth and functions | Soil water retention, nutrient cycling | Soil compaction, drought | Health | Individual life |
| Decay\* | Grow structure that provides substrates for leaf, flowers and other organs. | Provide hollows, dead wood, and bark for arboreal dwellers to use as habitat[^17] | Pruning, restricted growing space | Health | Individual life |
| Grow | Adapt to local environment | Cast shade, intercept rain, and alter microclimates[^19] | Uniform planting practices | Autonomy | Collective interaction |
| Resist | Develop structures that can resist change | Create microrefugia in modified landscapes such as cities[^20] and paddocks[^21] | Removal of branches deemed hazardous by humans | Autonomy | Collective interaction |
| Signal\* | Exchange resources through fungal networks in soil | Build resilience to shocks in arboreal communitiess[^8] | Soil sterilization, fungicide use | Affiliation: | Collective interaction |
| Host | Offer surfaces for symbiotes such as epiphytes and lichens | Create three dimensional variation in niches[^22], | Simplification of tree structure | Affiliation: | Collective interaction |
| Release | Release pollen and seed | Provide food source | Lack of pollinators, seed dispersers |  |  |
| Propagate\* | Recruit new trees across suitable ground | Renew canopy services across time[^11] | Propagate\* | Affiliation | Multiple generations |

## Relational indicators

We next provide further information on our relational indicators. These indicators measure relational conditions inside the habitat volume that make a subset of capabilities available. Each indicator uses a three‑part code x.y.z where x marks persona, y marks capability and z marks the specific indicator. Each indicator pairs with one effort metric. We track three effort metrics: canopy volume released from human control; the number of supporting structures deployed; or area converted for non‑human use.

**Table 4. Indicators**

| Indicator | What it measures | Raw VTK query | Raw schema row | Reporting status | Stream share |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Bird.acquire.peeling-bark` | Peeling bark volume | `stat_peeling bark > 0` | sub-indicator | kept | 100% of `Bird.acquire` |
| `Bird.communicate.perch-branch` | Perchable branch volume in senescing, snag, or artificial canopy | `stat_perch branch > 0 AND forest_size in senescing\|snag\|artificial` | sub-indicator | kept | 100% of `Bird.communicate` |
| `Bird.reproduce.hollow` | Hollow volume | `stat_hollow > 0` | sub-indicator | kept | 100% of `Bird.reproduce` |
| `Lizard.acquire.grass` | Low vegetation ground | `search_bioavailable == low-vegetation` | sub-indicator | kept | 33.3% of `Lizard.acquire` |
| `Lizard.acquire.dead-branch` | Dead branch volume | `stat_dead branch > 0` | sub-indicator | kept | 33.3% of `Lizard.acquire` |
| `Lizard.acquire.epiphyte` | Epiphyte volume | `stat_epiphyte > 0` | sub-indicator | kept | 33.3% of `Lizard.acquire` |
| `Lizard.acquire` | Combined acquire habitat | union of `grass`, `dead-branch`, and `epiphyte` | composite union | dropped | rebuilt from retained sub-indicators |
| `Lizard.communicate.not-paved` | Ground or open space that is not roadway, busy roadway, or parking | `(search_bioavailable in low-vegetation\|open space) AND NOT(search_urban_elements in roadway\|busy roadway\|parking)` | sub-indicator | kept | 100% of `Lizard.communicate` |
| `Lizard.reproduce.nurse-log` | Fallen log volume | `stat_fallen log > 0` | sub-indicator | kept | 50% of `Lizard.reproduce` |
| `Lizard.reproduce.fallen-tree` | Fallen or decayed tree volume | `forest_size in fallen\|decayed` | sub-indicator | kept | 50% of `Lizard.reproduce` |
| `Lizard.reproduce` | Combined reproduce habitat | union of `nurse-log` and `fallen-tree` | composite union | dropped | rebuilt from retained sub-indicators |
| `Tree.acquire.moderated` | Reduced pruning support | `proposal_release_control_intervention == reduce-canopy-pruning` | sub-indicator | dropped | excluded from stream graph |
| `Tree.acquire.autonomous` | Eliminated pruning support | `proposal_release_control_intervention == eliminate-canopy-pruning` | sub-indicator | kept | 100% of `Tree.acquire` after exclusions |
| `Tree.acquire` | Combined acquire habitat | union of `moderated` and `autonomous` | composite union | dropped | rebuilt from retained sub-indicators |
| `Tree.communicate.snag` | Snag volume | `forest_size == snag` | sub-indicator | kept | 33.3% of `Tree.communicate` |
| `Tree.communicate.fallen` | Fallen tree volume | `forest_size == fallen` | sub-indicator | kept | 33.3% of `Tree.communicate` |
| `Tree.communicate.decayed` | Decayed tree volume | `forest_size == decayed` | sub-indicator | kept | 33.3% of `Tree.communicate` |
| `Tree.communicate` | Combined communicate habitat | union of `snag`, `fallen`, and `decayed` | composite union | dropped | rebuilt from retained sub-indicators |
| `Tree.reproduce.smaller-patches-rewild` | Partial recruit intervention | `proposal_recruit_intervention == rewild-smaller-patch` | sub-indicator | dropped | excluded from stream graph |
| `Tree.reproduce.larger-patches-rewild` | Full recruit intervention | `proposal_recruit_intervention == rewild-larger-patch` | sub-indicator | kept | 100% of `Tree.reproduce` after exclusions |
| `Tree.reproduce` | Combined reproduce habitat | union of `smaller-patches-rewild` and `larger-patches-rewild` | composite union | dropped | rebuilt from retained sub-indicators |

We next provide an example of how the model tracks indicators within the habitat volume (Figure 4).


![The habitat volume for the Boulevard site across three different states. Voxels that do not contain indicators for lizard capabilities have been hidden. **Top:** **Current state**. Some voxels contain explore indicators (pink), but few voxels contain other indicators. **Middle:** **Trending pathway, 60 years**. The habitat volume after 60 years of current management shows similar indicators to existing conditions. **Bottom:** **Positive pathway, 60 years**. The habitat volume contains explore indicators plus significant grasslands related to lizard foraging (orange) and fallen logs and trees related to lizard shelter (green).](./media/image4.png)


The area of grassland (2.1.1) as well as the volume of dead branches (2.1.2) and epiphytes (2.1.3) in tree canopies relate to the lizard's capability to forage (Figure 4, orange). Humans can enable opportunities for lizards to express this capability by converting ground surfaces to grasslands (2.1.1), releasing tree canopies from human control to allow dead branches to develop (2.1.2), and installing native mistletoe in tree canopies (2.1.3).

The area of unpaved ground relates to the lizard's capability to explore (2.2.1) (Figure 4, pink). Humans can provide opportunities for exploration through removing hard surfaces. Sheltered sites including fallen nurse logs (2.3.1) and fallen trees (2.3.2) relate to the lizard's capability to shelter (Figure 4, green). Humans can support this capability through retaining fallen branches (2.3.1) and trees (2.3.2) in situ.
